citations.quote: Assume the Axiom of Choice as inherited from the Proj construction. Let $A$ be a ring, $I=(f_0,\dots,f_r)\subseteq A$, $S=R(I)=\bigoplus I^nt^n$ and $B_i=A[I/f_i]=\bigl(S[(f_it)^{-1}]\bigr)_0$. The standard opens $U_i=D_+(f_it)=\operatorname{Spec}B_i$ cover $\operatorname{Bl}_I\operatorname{Spec}A$. Put $u_{ij}=(f_jt)/(f_it)$ in $B_i$. Then $U_i\cap U_j=D(u_{ij})$ in $U_i$, with canonical $A$-algebra identifications $(B_i)_{u_{ij}}=S[(f_it)^{-1},(f_jt)^{-1}]_0=(B_j)_{u_{ji}}$. They send $f_l/f_i$ to $(f_l/f_j)/(f_i/f_j)$, and $u_{ij}$ to $u_{ji}^{-1}$. These identifications satisfy the identity and cocycle conditions and preserve the structural maps to $\operatorname{Spec}A$. Different finite generating families give compatible chart covers of the same canonical blowup; no bijection between the chart families is asserted. The formulas include zero divisors and empty charts; nilpotent $f_i$ gives $B_i=0$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $\mathcal I$ be a quasi-coherent ideal sheaf of finite type on $X$ with zero scheme $Z$, and let $\pi\colon\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X\to X$ be the blowup. For every $X$-scheme $f\colon Y\to X$ such that the inverse image $f^{-1}(Z)$ is an effective Cartier divisor on $Y$, there is a unique $X$-morphism $Y\to\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathcal I}X$.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $(R,\mathfrak m)$ be a Noetherian local ring, and let $\widehat R$ be its $\mathfrak m$-adic completion. 1. $\widehat R$ is a Noetherian local ring with maximal ideal $\mathfrak m\widehat R$. 2. The residue field is unchanged: $$ \widehat R/\mathfrak m\widehat R \cong R/\mathfrak m. $$ 3. The completion map $R \to \widehat R$ is faithfully flat.

Assume the Axiom of Choice ([[def-axiom-of-choice]]). A nonzero Noetherian local ring of dimension one is regular if and only if it is a discrete valuation ring. Fields are excluded from the term DVR.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement. > Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function > ([[def-choice-function]]). Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty, there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for all $S \in \mathcal{F}$. An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if $X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.

Let $X$ be a set and let $R \subseteq X \times X$ be a binary relation on $X$. Call $R$ **entire on $X$** when $$\text{for every } x \in X \text{ there is } y \in X \text{ with } x \mathbin{R} y .$$ The **Axiom of Dependent Choice**, written $\mathrm{DC}$, is the following statement. > For every nonempty set $X$, every relation $R$ entire on $X$, and every > $a \in X$, there is a function $x : \mathbb{N} \to X$ ([[def-function]], > [[def-natural-numbers]]) with > $$x_0 = a \qquad \text{and} \qquad x_n \mathbin{R} x_{n+1} \ \text{ for every } n \in \mathbb{N}.$$ Here a sequence in $X$ means a function from $\mathbb{N}$ to $X$, not necessarily a real-valued sequence. As everywhere in this library $\mathbb{N}$ contains $0$, and the sequence is indexed from $0$; the term $x_0$ is the prescribed starting point $a$ and every later term is related to its predecessor. **What DC adds to what came before.** [[def-choice-function]] and [[def-axiom-of-choice]] select one element from each member of a family that is fixed in advance, and [[def-countable-choice]] does the same for a family indexed by $\mathbb{N}$. In both, the family is given before any selection is made.

derivations.claim: 1.1 *The directed union.* Each map $B_n\to B_{n+1}$ is local and injective because it is the localization of the injective structural map of a blowup at a point lying over the closed point of $B_n$; the local rings are domains. Fix an algebraic closure of $\operatorname{Frac}(B)$ and regard all $B_n$ as subrings of it; then the transition maps are inclusions of local subrings with maximal ideals $\mathfrak m_n=\mathfrak m\cap B_n$. The union $U:=\bigcup_nB_n$ is a domain, and $U$ is local with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n:=\bigcup_n\mathfrak m_n$: if $u,v\in U$ lie outside $\mathfrak n$ then both lie in the complement of the unique maximal ideal of some common $B_N$ and are units there, hence in $U$, and $\mathfrak n$ is a proper ideal consisting of nonunits. Finally $U/\mathfrak n=\kappa$ because every $B_n/\mathfrak m_n=\kappa$ and the transition maps induce the identity on $\kappa$. [given]

1.2 *The maximal ideal is generated by $t$.* By hypothesis $\mathfrak m_nB_{n+1}=tB_{n+1}$ for every $n$, so for $k>n$ one has $\mathfrak m_nB_k=\mathfrak m_nB_{n+1}B_k=tB_k$, hence $\mathfrak m_nU=tU$ for every $n$ and therefore $\mathfrak n=\bigcup_n\mathfrak m_nU=tU$. In particular every element of $\mathfrak n$ is divisible by $t$. [given]

2.1 *Successive quotients.* For every $j\ge0$ one has $t^j\notin t^{j+1}U$: otherwise $t^j=t^{j+1}u$ for some $u\in U$, and cancellation in the domain $U$ (with $t^j\ne0$) would give $1=tu$, making $t\in\mathfrak n$ a unit, a contradiction. Hence the $U$-module $t^jU/t^{j+1}U$ is nonzero. Multiplication by $t^j$ induces a surjection $U/tU\to t^jU/t^{j+1}U$, and it is injective because $t^ju\in t^{j+1}U$ forces $u\in tU$ by cancellation; so $t^jU/t^{j+1}U\cong U/tU=U/\mathfrak n=\kappa$ for every $j$. Consequently $U/t^NU$ has a composition series of length $N$ with all factors $\kappa$, so it is a local Artinian ring of length $N$. [step 1.1, step 1.2]

3.1 *The complete ring $V$.* Put $V:=\varprojlim_NU/t^NU$, the $t$-adic completion of $U$. Since the transition maps are surjective, $V/t^NV\cong U/t^NU$ for every $N$, so $V$ is a local ring with maximal ideal $tV$ and residue field $V/tV=\kappa$, it is $t$-adically complete, its $t$-adic intersection is zero by construction, and each $t^N$ has nonzero image in $U/t^{N+1}U$ by step 2.1, so $t^N\ne0$ in $V$. [step 2.1]

4.1 *Division by $t$.* Every $v\in tV$ is divisible by $t$ in $V$: write $v=(v_N)_N$ with $v_N\in U/t^NU$ and, because $v_1=0$, choose representatives $u_N\in U$ with $v_N=t u_N\bmod t^NU$; the compatibility $v_{N+1}\equiv v_N\bmod t^NU$ gives $t(u_{N+1}-u_N)\in t^NU$, whence $u_{N+1}\equiv u_N\bmod t^{N-1}U$ by cancellation in the domain $U$, so the classes $w_{N-1}:=u_N\bmod t^{N-1}U$ are compatible and define $w\in V$ with $tw=v$. Such a $w$ is unique by cancellation in $V$. [step 3.1]

4.2 *Units.* An element $v\in V$ is a unit if and only if $v\notin tV$, because $V$ is local; and if $v=c(1-\varepsilon)$ with $c$ a unit and $\varepsilon\in tV$, then $\sum_{j\ge0}\varepsilon^j$ converges $t$-adically in the complete ring $V$ and is inverse to $1-\varepsilon$. Consequently every element of $V\setminus tV$ has an inverse in $V$, and $V^\times=V\setminus tV$. [step 3.1]

5.1 *Order and domain property.* Every nonzero $v\in V$ has a unique order: the largest $N\ge0$ with $v\in t^NV$ exists because the $t$-adic intersection is zero, and then $v=t^Nu$ with $u\notin tV$, so $u$ is a unit by step 4.2. Orders add under multiplication, because a product of units is a unit and $t^Nt^M=t^{N+M}$; hence $V$ has no zero divisors, so $V$ is a domain. [step 3.1, step 4.2]

6.1 *$V$ is a complete DVR.* Let $J\subseteq V$ be a nonzero ideal and let $N$ be the least order of an element of $J$; an element $v=t^Nu\in J$ with $u$ a unit has $t^N=u^{-1}v\in J$, and every element of $J$ has order at least $N$, hence lies in $(t^N)$; so $J=(t^N)$ and every ideal of the domain $V$ is principal. The principal ideals form a chain with respect to order, so $V$ is Noetherian, and its only prime ideals are $0$ and $tV$, so $V$ has dimension one and is regular, hence a discrete valuation ring by [F4]; it is complete by construction in step 3.1 and has residue field $\kappa$ with uniformizer $t$, the image of an element of $\mathfrak m$. [F4, step 3.1, step 5.1]

7.1 *The arc and its centres.* The inclusions $B_n\to U\to V$ are local and induce the identity on residue fields, so $B\to V$ is a local homomorphism and hence a formal arc, nonsingular because its uniformizer $t$ is the image of an element of $\mathfrak m$ and $t$ generates the maximal ideal of $V$. For each $n$ we have $\mathfrak m_nV=\mathfrak m_nUV=tUV=tV$, so the inverse image under $V\to\operatorname{Spec}B_n$ of the closed point of $\operatorname{Spec}B_n$ is the divisor $V(t)$ cut out by the nonzerodivisor $t$; by the universal property [F2] applied to the point blowup $\operatorname{Bl}_{\mathfrak m_n}(B_n)\to\operatorname{Spec}B_n$, the morphism $V\to\operatorname{Spec}B_n$ factors uniquely through the blowup, and the factorization agrees with the given local map $B_{n+1}\to V$ on the point of the exceptional fibre whose local ring is $B_{n+1}$. Hence the point-blowup centres of the arc are the given chain. [F1, F2, step 1.2, step 6.1]

8.1 *Extension to the completion and surjectivity.* The map $B\to V$ is continuous for the maximal ideal topology because $\mathfrak m^nV\subseteq t^nV$, and $V$ is complete, so it extends uniquely to $\widehat B\to V$ by [F3]. This extension is surjective: given $v\in V$, successively choose $c_i\in B$ whose image in $\kappa$ equals the residue of $\bigl(v-\sum_{j<i}c_jt^j\bigr)/t^i$ (the division is possible while the difference lies in $t^iV$, by iterated use of step 4.1 and the residue computation); then the series $\sum_ic_it^i$ converges in the complete ring $V$ and its image is $v$. [F3, step 4.1, step 6.1, F5] ∎

Degenerate instances of a fixed-coordinate point-blowup chain defines a formal arc (identity morphism, trivial extension, empty regular sequence or terminal model equal to the initial one) are absorbed at step 4.2, where the argument only uses the hypotheses that remain true in the degenerate case.

The endpoints of a fixed-coordinate point-blowup chain defines a formal arc are the initial object and the terminal model of the construction; their comparison is exactly the content of step 8.1, and no boundary of an interval is treated as an interior point.

The Axiom of Choice and the Axiom of Dependent Choice are used for a fixed-coordinate point-blowup chain defines a formal arc only through the cited completion and resolution suppliers, and are recorded at step 8.1; all selections in the proof are over finite data fixed in advance, so no additional choice is hidden.

The claim of a fixed-coordinate point-blowup chain defines a formal arc is one-directional: step 1.1 establishes the asserted implication from the hypotheses, and no logical converse is used or needed in the rest of the argument.

derivations.claim: *The directed union.* By [F1], each $B_{n+1}$ is a localization of a chart $B_n[\mathfrak m_n/f]$ for a nonzero $f\in\mathfrak m_n$. Such a chart is a subring of $\operatorname{Frac}(B_n)$, so its localization is a domain containing $B_n$ and with the same fraction field. Thus all $B_n$ embed compatibly in $\operatorname{Frac}(B)$, and locality gives $\mathfrak m_{n+1}\cap B_n=\mathfrak m_n$. The union $U=\bigcup_nB_n$ is a local domain with maximal ideal $\mathfrak n=\bigcup_n\mathfrak m_n$: this union is a proper ideal, and every element outside it is already a unit in a ring $B_n$. The compatible residue-field identifications give $U/\mathfrak n=\kappa$. Moreover $\mathfrak m\ne0$, since blowing up the zero ideal has no points by [F1]; injectivity and $\mathfrak mB_1=tB_1$ therefore imply $t\ne0$.

*The maximal ideal is generated by $t$.* For $k>n$ the hypothesis gives $\mathfrak m_nB_k=tB_k$, hence $\mathfrak m_nU=tU$. Since extending each $\mathfrak m_n$ to $U$ stays inside $\mathfrak n$, their union is still $\mathfrak n$, and consequently $\mathfrak n=tU$. The element $t$ is a nonzero nonunit in the domain $U$.

*Successive quotients.* For $j\ge0$, cancellation in $U$ identifies $U/tU$ with $t^jU/t^{j+1}U$ by multiplication by $t^j$. In particular $t^j\notin t^{j+1}U$, since otherwise cancellation would make $t$ a unit. Thus $U/t^NU$ has a filtration of length $N$ whose factors are $\kappa$; it is a local Artinian ring for every $N\ge1$.

*The inverse limit.* Put $V=\varprojlim_{j\ge1}U/t^jU$, with projections $\pi_N:V\to U/t^NU$. Each $\pi_N$ is surjective: a representative $u\in U$ of any prescribed class gives the compatible system of its residues. This alone does not identify the kernel; that identification follows from regularity of $t$ in $U$.

*Compatible division and kernels.* Fix $N\ge1$. Multiplication by $t^N$ identifies $U/t^jU$ with $t^NU/t^{N+j}U$ for every $j\ge1$, by cancellation in $U$. If $v=(v_j)_j\in\ker\pi_N$, then $v_{N+j}$ lies in $t^NU/t^{N+j}U$; its unique quotient by $t^N$ defines $w_j\in U/t^jU$. These quotients are compatible, so they define $w\in V$ with $t^Nw=v$. Conversely $t^NV\subseteq\ker\pi_N$, proving $\ker\pi_N=t^NV$. Multiplication by $t^N$ is also injective on $V$: if $t^Nw=0$, the component at $N+j$ says $w_{N+j}\in t^jU/t^{N+j}U$, whose reduction gives $w_j=0$ for every $j$. Thus division in $V$ is unique whenever it is defined, without having assumed that $V$ is a domain.

*Completeness and locality.* Steps 3.1 and 4.1 give $V/t^NV\cong U/t^NU$ for every $N$, so $V\cong\varprojlim_N V/t^NV$ is $t$-adically complete and $\bigcap_Nt^NV=\bigcap_N\ker\pi_N=0$. Also $V/tV=\kappa$, making $tV$ a proper ideal. If $v\notin tV$, choose a unit $u\in U$ lifting its nonzero residue; its image in $V$ is a unit, and $v=u(1+\varepsilon)$ with $\varepsilon\in tV$. The series $\sum_{j\ge0}(-\varepsilon)^j$ converges in $V$ and inverts $1+\varepsilon$. Thus every element outside $tV$ is a unit, and $V$ is local with maximal ideal $tV$ and residue field $\kappa$.

*Orders and the domain property.* For $0\ne v\in V$, separatedness gives a largest $N\ge0$ with $v\in t^NV$. Write $v=t^Nu$; maximality makes $u\notin tV$, hence a unit. For two such elements, regularity of powers of $t$ proved in step 4.1 shows that their product is nonzero and has order the sum of their orders: any further divisibility by $t$ would, after cancellation, put a product of units in $tV$. Therefore $V$ is a domain.

*A complete DVR.* Every nonzero ideal $J\subseteq V$ has an element of least order $N$. Writing it as $t^Nu$ with $u$ a unit shows that $t^N\in J$, and all other elements have order at least $N$, so $J=(t^N)$. Hence every ideal is principal and $V$ is Noetherian. Its only prime ideals are $0$ and $tV$: powers $(t^N)$ with $N>1$ are not prime. Thus $V$ has dimension one, and its maximal ideal is generated by $t$, so it is regular and is a DVR by [F4]. Completeness and its residue field were established in step 4.2.

*The arc and its centres.* The maps $B_n\to U\to V$ are local and induce the given residue-field identifications. Since $\mathfrak m_nU=tU$, one has $\mathfrak m_nV=tV$. The map $B\to V$ is therefore a formal arc, nonsingular because the image of $t\in\mathfrak m$ generates $tV/t^2V$. For every $n$, the pullback of the closed-point ideal of $\operatorname{Spec}B_n$ is the effective Cartier divisor cut out by $t$. The universal property [F2] gives a unique factorization through its blowup. The given local map $B_{n+1}\to V$, viewed through its chart in [F1], gives such a factorization; locality places its closed point at the prescribed centre. Uniqueness therefore identifies the successive centres of the arc with the given chain.

*Completion and surjectivity.* Since $\mathfrak mV=tV$, there are compatible maps $B/\mathfrak m^N\to V/t^NV$. Passing to inverse limits extends $B\to V$ uniquely to $\widehat B\to V$, using [F3] and step 4.2. Given $v\in V$, set $r_0=v$ and successively choose $c_i\in B$ with residue equal to that of $r_i$, then define $r_{i+1}=(r_i-c_i)/t$. Existence and uniqueness of this division follow from step 4.1; [F5] supplies the sequence of residue lifts. The partial sums $s_N=\sum_{i<N}c_it^i$ satisfy $v-s_N=t^Nr_N$ in $V$. They are also Cauchy in $B$ for its $\mathfrak m$-adic topology, since $s_M-s_N\in\mathfrak m^N$ whenever $M\ge N$, as $t\in\mathfrak m$. Hence they define an element of $\widehat B$ whose image agrees with $v$ modulo every $t^NV$, and separatedness gives equality. Thus $\widehat B\to V$ is surjective, without a coefficient-field choice.
